extracted.intended_audience: citizens and delegates evaluating the proposed U.S. Constitution (readers of The Federalist / informed public of New York, 1788)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging whether a proposed constitution is republican, whether it is federal or national in character, whether the convention was authorized to propose it, and whether the powers conferred are necessary and safe. Focuses on foundation, sources, operation, extent of powers, amendment procedure, tenure of offices, and necessity/justification of deviations from commission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a republic
rubrics_metrics.description: A republic is (or may be described as) 'a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people, and is administered by persons holding their offices during pleasure, for a limited period, or during good behavior.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential: government must be derived from the great body of society, not from an inconsiderable proportion or favored class. Sufficient: persons administering it are appointed directly or indirectly by the people and hold appointments by one of the tenures specified (during pleasure, for a limited period, or during good behavior). Avoid counting governments as republican simply because they bear the name; examine origin of authority and tenure of officeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republican-compliance indicators in constitutional structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete institutional features by which the plan conforms 'in the most rigid sense' to a republican standard: direct election of the House of Representatives; indirect election of the Senate; indirect derivation of the President from the people's choice; remote choice of judges and other officers; defined tenures (periodic elections and tenure by good behavior for judges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare terms to State constitutions (e.g., House two years, Senate six years, President four years). Check explicit prohibitions (e.g., prohibition of titles of nobility) and guarantees (express guaranty of republican form to each State). Use the listed parallels to state practice as evidence of republican character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation criterion for federal vs national character
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the constitution's foundation is 'federal' or 'national' by asking whether assent and ratification are given by the people as distinct and independent States or by the people as one aggregate nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ratification is the unanimous assent of several States, given as sovereign bodies (or by their own peoples acting in state capacity), the act is federal; if it is the decision of a majority of the overall people binding minorities, it is national. Examine the mode of ratification (by States vs aggregate popular majority) to classify foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-of-powers criterion (where ordinary powers are drawn)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether ordinary powers of government are derived from the people (national) or from the States as political/coequal societies (federal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect how each branch's powers are sourced: e.g., House derives powers from the people (national feature); Senate derives appointment from States (federal feature); executive is from a compound source. Mixed sourcing signals a mixed (neither purely national nor purely federal) character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operation-of-powers criterion (on whom powers operate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate federal vs national by whether powers operate on the political bodies composing the Confederacy (states in their political capacities) or on individual citizens in their individual capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If powers act primarily on states (collective political bodies), that is federal; if they act on individuals directly (ordinary proceedings, law, taxation, criminal jurisdiction, etc.), that is national. Record exceptions (cases where states are parties) but classify by ordinary operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent-of-powers criterion (scope and supremacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge national vs federal character by extent of powers: a national government implies indefinite supremacy over persons and things (supreme national legislature), whereas a federal government has enumerated powers and leaves residuary sovereignty to the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether jurisdiction is enumerated and limited (federal) or indefinite and supreme (national). Note that some mixed forms may have national operation but federal extent (e.g., enumerated national powers with residual state sovereignty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment-mode criterion (how amendments are introduced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify by the authoritative mode for amendments: a wholly national government would have ultimate authority in a majority of the people; a wholly federal one would require concurrence of each State. The proposed plan's mode (requiring more than a majority, computing proportions by states, permitting less than unanimous concurrence) makes it neither wholly national nor wholly federal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine thresholds (majority of people vs concurrence of all states vs intermediate formulas). How proportions are computed (by states or citizens) affects classification. Consider whether the amendment procedure leans toward federalism or national supremacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of the convention (bounds of commission and permissible alterations)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether the convention was authorized to frame the proposed government, inspect commissions given (Annapolis recommendation, Congress resolution) and ask whether the convention's mandate to propose 'alterations and provisions' encompassed the changes made or whether those changes amounted to a 'transmutation' beyond authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply two rules of construction: give some meaning to every part of the expression; where parts conflict, sacrifice the less important to the more important (ends over means). Assess whether proposed 'alterations and provisions' reasonably include insertion of new articles and substantial reforms necessary to form 'a firm national government adequate to the exigencies of the Union.' Mark the boundary between permitted alterations and usurpation by asking whether the change is necessary to secure the constitutional end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normative duty to exceed strict commission in exigent circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the convention exceeded its formal commission, consider whether necessity, public interest, and extraordinary circumstances justified exercising assumed powers to propose a constitution that would secure the nation's safety and happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh context: urgency of national crisis, public expectation, prior assumptions (Annapolis, Congressional recommendations), and historical precedents of informal proposals. The approbation of the people (ratification) can retroactively legitimize irregularities. Avoid formalistic rejection when substance protects public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity and proportionality of conferred powers
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating whether powers conferred on the general government are proper, first ask whether each power is a 'necessary means' to an identified end; then consider safeguards against abuse and whether the aggregate power endangers state jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject powers simply because they admit potential abuse; judge whether they are necessary to achieve public good (choose the greater good). After finding necessity, consider guardrails (constitutional limits, judicial impartiality, enumerated powers) to mitigate perversion. Evaluate both individual powers and the aggregate mass of powers for danger to state sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of powers by object
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce the general government's powers into classes by the objects they serve to judge appropriateness: (1) Security against foreign danger; (2) Regulation of intercourse with foreign nations; (3) Maintenance of harmony and proper intercourse among the States; (4) (and implicitly) other classes relating to revenue, commerce, and national administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these object-classes to assess whether particular powers (e.g., trade regulation, standing armies, coinage, postal system, trials, taxation) are suitable for a general government. Consider historical practice and deficiencies under Confederation when assigning powers to these classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure, terms, and impeachment as republican metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate republican character by concrete tenure rules: periodic elections (House two years), Senate six years, President four years, judges holding by 'good behavior', and presidential impeachability at any time during office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare proposed terms with state constitutions (examples cited: South Carolina, Maryland, New York, Virginia, Delaware). Assess whether tenures secure popular accountability and independent judiciaries consistent with republican principles. Note impeachment provisions as check on executive power (contrast with states where chief magistrate was not impeachable in office).
